title: Root location and sign changes
terms: Root Location theorem; Intermediate Value theorem; sign change; root isolation.

exposition.text:
A real polynomial is continuous. If p(a) and p(b) have opposite signs, the Intermediate Value
theorem guarantees at least one root strictly between a and b. Disjoint sign-changing intervals
give distinct roots. Combined with the degree bound, enough such intervals can establish the
exact number of roots without solving for them.
The absence of a sign change does not imply absence of a root: an even-multiplicity root can
merely touch the axis. A sign change alone gives existence, not uniqueness; monotonicity or a
degree count supplies additional information. Every real polynomial of odd degree has a real
root because its two tails have opposite signs.

question.text:
A quartic real polynomial satisfies p(−2) > 0, p(−1) < 0, p(0) > 0, p(1) < 0, and p(2) > 0. How
many distinct real roots does it have?
(A) 1 (B) 2 (C) 3 (D) 4 (E) Cannot be determined

solution.text:
Each of the four disjoint intervals (−2, −1), (−1, 0), (0, 1), and (1, 2) contains a root.
Degree 4 permits at most four distinct roots. Therefore there are exactly four, each simple.

As x → −∞, a monic cubic tends to −∞, whereas p(−1) > 0. Continuity forces a root be-
low −1. The stated values also force roots in (−1, 0) and (0, 1), exhausting the three roots.

The derivative is 3(x − 1), with a local maximum at −1 of value a + 2 and a local mini-
mum at 1 of value a − 2. The three monotonic intervals each contain a root precisely when
the maximum is positive and minimum negative: −2 < a < 2. At the endpoints a root is
repeated.

question.text:
A real polynomial p satisfies p(0) < 0 < p(1) and has no zeros at either endpoint. Which must
hold for its roots in (0, 1)?
(A) There is exactly one distinct root.
(B) Every root has odd multiplicity.
(C) The sum of the multiplicities is odd.
(D) There are at least three roots counting multiplicity.
(E) The derivative is nonzero at every root.

solution.text:
Crossing a real root reverses the sign exactly when its multiplicity is odd. Since the end-
point signs differ, the total multiplicity of the roots crossed must be odd. Additional
even-multiplicity roots or several odd-multiplicity roots are possible, so uniqueness and
simplicity do not follow.
